channel.title: Prometheus devlog
channel.description: Building Prometheus, a custom 2.5D engine and editor, on the way to Forgotten Memories, Endless Abyss.

item.title: Catching up: two months of Prometheus
item.description:
Two months and a little over 1,800 commits in, this is where Prometheus stands, with links to the posts that go deeper. It ends with why development is pausing for a rebuild.

Quick reminder of the goal: Prometheus is a custom 2.5D engine with a browser-based editor. The world is fully 3D; the characters and props in it are 2D pixel-art sprites. Everything is being built toward Forgotten Memories, Endless Abyss, an online MMO set in an endless dungeon that reshapes itself around how its players behave. The game itself is still a future milestone. Right now the work is the engine and the tools.

The editor and the server

The editor is a remote session into a backend that owns the simulation. The browser renders locally and trades state snapshots with the server rather than streaming video. In September that hit its first real milestone: two browser tabs editing the same scene at once, with undo carrying across them and nothing lost when a tab refreshes mid-edit. The same simulation package runs on the server in the editor and locally in an exported game, so what you test is what ships. More in The server owns the world.

On top of that there's now most of what you'd expect from a scene editor: a hierarchy and inspector, a four-pane quad view, lights and shadows, materials, post-processing, particle effects (campfires with flames, smoke and embers, wall torches, lightning), Rapier physics, and camera rails for fly-throughs. Scenes keep a version history you can preview and roll back, and the editor recovers unsaved edits after a crash.

Every feature that lands also goes into one showcase scene, Re-Forged, which has a guided tour that walks through the engine feature by feature. It's the scene in the screenshot above, and it's how I check that new work actually reaches the screen and doesn't just pass its tests.

Frieze: from 3D models to pixel sprites

Every sprite in the game starts life as a real 3D model. Frieze imports the model, borrows animation clips from a shared library and retargets them to the model's rig, then captures it from several angles and bakes the result into pixel-art sprite sheets. It has its own palettes, a pixel editor for touch-ups, and batch re-baking when a source changes. More in Frieze: pixel art from 3D models.

The sprites also bake a normal map, so a flat sprite catches light from the 3D scene around it: a torch on its left lights its left side. The whole route, from importing a model to baking it, publishing it and placing it in a scene, is now one workflow with a readable report at each step.

Walking around: Delve

Delve is the first mode where you actually walk around: a third-person camera at a 35° tilt following a sprite character, with the billboards turning to face the camera and switching animation frames as they move. The first stress test put fifty animated billboards in a scene and held a mean of 12.7 ms per frame on my desktop. That's a dev machine, not a phone, so it's a baseline, not a verdict. More in First steps in Delve.

The gameplay foundation

None of this is gameplay yet, but most of what gameplay will stand on now exists (more in Teaching sprites to think):

  • Input: keyboard, mouse and gamepad, with rebinding.
  • UI: widgets and HUD panels with anchoring, focus and keyboard/gamepad navigation.
  • Scripting: script files edited in your own editor and watched from disk, with type checking, readable errors and shared scripts.
  • AI: behaviour trees with a shared blackboard, sensing and perception, navigation, and crowds that send a couple of hundred agents to one goal along a shared flow field.
  • Systems: physics queries and collision layers, an event bus, a game clock, sprite animation states, dialogue, localisation, entity pooling and a component model.

Built for phones

The game is aimed at mobile, so the editor measures every scene against a device budget: triangles, draw calls, texture memory, sprite sheets and entity counts, each checked against mobile, browser and desktop limits. The world is split into regions that load and unload around the camera, so distant areas give their memory back and come back intact when you return. A scene can also be exported as a static build that runs with no backend at all. More, including the first numbers from real phones, in Will it run on a phone?

What's next: a pause to rebuild

Two decisions have changed the plan. The editor is moving into a desktop app built on Electron, and the platform is becoming plugin-based, so features plug into a core rather than being built into it. Together those mean a full rewrite. So development is on pause while I rework: new designs in Figma, and the platform redesigned from the plugin perspective from the ground up.

The engine work is more or less done. What it needs now is more thought about how to make the rest of the game a reality on top of it. The biggest piece of that thinking is the living world. The dungeon won't be a complete map hidden under fog; ground that nobody has reached doesn't exist yet. Terrain is generated as players, and monsters, actually travel into it. A monster wandering off on its own extends the world along the path it walks, without revealing that ground to anyone. What each player has discovered stays private to them, while the terrain itself is shared by everyone. More in A world that isn't there yet.

Three stores, one launch

Beyond the editor, the game still needs a mobile version for the App Store and Google Play, and a Steam version for PC. All three will release at the same time. That's a substantial undertaking for a solo developer.

Not entirely solo

My teenagers are studying engineering and will, I hope, help me design and build the game world. A few friends are taking on the music and ambience, playing the first vertical slice as they write for it. That slice is the next real milestone: maybe later this year, maybe early 2027, we'll have something to show for all the hard work. There's a lot to do until then, so stand by.

item.title: Will it run on a phone?
item.description:
The game is meant for phones first, so this week was about finding out how far the engine is from that, with real numbers instead of hopes.

A budget you can see

The editor now measures a scene against a device budget (triangles, draw calls, texture memory, sprite sheets and entity counts) with separate limits for mobile, browser and desktop. The first time I pointed it at the showcase scene, it said texture memory was 78% over the mobile budget.

That turned out to be the meter: it was counting shared textures more than once. Counted properly, the scene was under budget all along. Phones still shouldn't download desktop-sized textures, though, so a new asset pipeline publishes a separate version of each texture per device, with phone textures capped at 512 pixels. On the showcase scene that takes texture memory from 131.9 MiB to 83.9 MiB on mobile, well inside the 192 MB budget.

Draw calls are the open problem. The showcase scene makes 178 of them, and the mobile limit is 100.

Streaming the world in

The world is split into regions. As the camera moves, nearby regions stay loaded, the next ones wait warm, and distant ones give back their memory, then come back intact when you return.

Exporting a game

A scene can now be exported as a static build: plain files that run in a browser with no server behind them, with the simulation running on the device. That's the shape a shipped game will take.

Real phones

Then the real test. A profiling page runs a fixed workload on the phone itself and records the results. I ran it on a Galaxy Z Fold7, folded and unfolded, and on an iPhone 14 Pro, against a hall of about 60 sprites.

The median frame came in right on 60 fps on the Fold7 (16.6 to 16.7 ms) and a little slower on the iPhone (19 to 21 ms). The slowest frames ran past the 60 fps budget on both. Treat these as early samples rather than benchmarks, but the verdict is clear enough: close, not there yet, and now it's something I can measure instead of guess.

item.title: Teaching sprites to think
item.description:
The last few weeks went into the systems game logic will be written on. The last pieces of a first set landed today, so here's a tour.

Scripts are files

Game scripts are ordinary files, so I write them in VS Code instead of a text box in the editor. With file watching on, saving in VS Code reloads the script in the running editor. Scripts are type-checked, errors show up where I can see them, and a script that throws no longer drags the frame down with it.

Behaviour trees

Characters run behaviour trees: small graphs of decisions like "if you can see the player, approach; otherwise wander". Trees share a blackboard, a set of named values characters can read and write, which is how two characters can hold a conversation or a group can coordinate.

Seeing and hearing

A character can have a view cone, a hearing range and a memory, and its behaviour tree reads them. In the editor I can show the cone and the hearing ring and tune them live.

Getting around, together

Characters find routes across the navigation grid. Crowds go one better. When many characters head for the same goal, the engine builds one flow field, a grid of arrows pointing the way, and they all read it instead of each searching for its own route. In a test with 200 characters heading for one goal, that meant zero route searches per second and at most one field build.

Talking

There's a dialogue system too: lines, choices and branches, with the camera able to move to whoever is speaking. The first test conversation in the showcase scene goes: "You found the stairs. Most people forget them." Choose "I remember." and the reply is "Then the abyss remembers you too."

And the rest

Gamepads and rebindable controls, UI widgets and HUD panels, an event bus, a game clock, localisation, collision layers, physics queries for AI, and entity pooling so a burst of spawns doesn't stall a frame. None of it is a game yet. It's the toolbox the game will be built with.

item.title: A world that isn't there yet
item.description:
This week I pinned down one of the most important rules of the game world, and it changes what the engine has to do.

Ground that nobody has reached does not exist. It isn't hidden or fogged over; it hasn't been generated. The dungeon is endless, so it gets built as it's explored.

Monsters explore too

Monsters don't idle in rooms waiting for a player to show up. They wander, head home, follow routes, and keep doing it when no player is anywhere near. When a monster walks toward the edge of the known world, terrain is generated for its path, and only its path. It learns the ground it has actually walked, not a circle of everything around it, and none of that reveals anything to players.

Terrain is shared: once it exists, it exists for everyone. Maps aren't. What each player has discovered is theirs alone by default.

The rules that hold it together

A few engine rules fall out of that:

  • Nothing walks on nothing. Before any actor, player or monster, moves into new ground, that ground is generated and committed, with its collision and navigation. Nobody crosses a blank region, a guessed bridge or a floor that doesn't exist yet.
  • First come, first fixed. Once ground exists, it stays. Otherwise a monster could head home to its den and find a lake there, because a player's arrival had regenerated the area. A player who turns up later finds the same trails, dens and residents the monster left.
  • Budgets. An endlessly wandering monster could otherwise generate an endless world with nobody in it. Generation distance, active populations and simulation time all have limits, and when one runs out a monster waits at the edge rather than inventing ground.
  • Reproducible from history. A seed alone can't rebuild a world shaped by what happened in it, so the engine keeps the seed, the generator version, the behaviour that shaped the world and everything that was committed.
  • Not flat. Hills, valleys, cliffs, gaps and water. One spot on the map can hold a bridge above a cave, so a single height per point isn't enough.

Where it starts

None of this is gameplay yet. These are engine requirements, and the first building block arrived the same day: navigation. The editor can now bake a grid that says where an agent of a given size fits, and find a route across it.

Today that works on flat floors in scenes I've built by hand. Terrain that generates itself as monsters walk into it is the long road from here.

item.title: First steps in Delve
item.description:
Until this week, Prometheus was something you looked at. Now you can walk around in it.

Delve is the engine's first walking mode. A third-person camera tilted at 35° follows a sprite character, and every billboard in the scene turns to face the camera, picking the right direction and animation frame as it moves. It runs inside the editor, so I can step into a scene I'm building, walk around it, and step back out to carry on editing.

Input that isn't tied to a keyboard

Delve brought the input system with it. Game code never asks "is W pressed?". It asks for actions like move and turn, and whatever the player is holding supplies them. On a keyboard that's the usual keys. On a touchscreen a virtual stick appears bottom-left, with turn buttons on the right:

Hide the editor around it and what's left is what a player would see:

How heavy is a crowd of sprites?

Every billboard has to be turned, framed and positioned every frame, so I measured that early. Fifty animated billboards held a mean of 12.7 ms per frame on my desktop while I walked around them, about 79 frames a second. That's a development machine, not a phone, so it's a baseline to measure later work against rather than a verdict.

item.title: Frieze: pixel art from 3D models
item.description:
Every character and prop in Prometheus is a 2D pixel-art sprite standing in a 3D world. Drawing all of those by hand, from eight directions, for every animation, isn't something a solo developer can do. So the engine makes them. The tool is called Frieze.

Models in, sprite sheets out

Frieze takes a 3D model, poses it with animation clips, captures it from several angles and bakes each frame into pixel art at a fixed size, then packs the frames into a sprite sheet. Clips can come with the model or be borrowed from a shared library and retargeted to the model's skeleton, so one walk cycle can serve many characters.

It also works from 2D art. A drawing can be given joints and animated with the same library clips. For testing that I used a free character turnaround from OpenGameArt:

Palettes

A sheet can be indexed, so each colour belongs to a palette slot. Change a slot and the character changes colour everywhere it appears, with no new bake. The green-trousered character here is the same artwork as the blue one, with four of its thirteen palette slots changed:

Touching up by hand

Automatic isn't always right, so Frieze has a pixel editor built in, with onion skinning across frames. A bad frame can be fixed in place without leaving the tool or re-baking the sheet.

Sprites that catch the light

Each bake also produces a normal map, so a flat sprite reacts to the 3D lights around it: a campfire on its left lights its left side.

That led to my favourite bug so far. Seen from behind at a low angle, a character's shoes glowed white-hot, as if lit from inside:

The cause was in the sprite material. A tweak that softens how light wraps around a sprite was also being applied to its reflections, and at grazing angles that amplified the reflection enormously, even on a completely rough surface. Limiting the softening to diffuse light fixed it:

item.title: The server owns the world
item.description:
The editor passed its first real milestone today, so it's a good moment to explain the decision underneath it.

Two ways to put a game in a browser

The Prometheus editor runs in a web browser, but the scene lives on a server. There were two ways to build that.

Pixel streaming renders every frame on the server and streams video to the browser, the way cloud gaming does; the browser is a remote monitor. That costs a GPU video encoder per viewer, tens of megabits a second, text and thin lines softened by video compression, and input lag on every click.

State streaming keeps the renderer in the browser. The server runs the authoritative simulation (physics, behaviour, game rules) and sends compact updates about what changed; the browser draws them locally and sends edits back. The research I did put that at a few hundred times less bandwidth than video, with no server GPU per viewer and a UI that responds at local speed.

Prometheus streams state.

One simulation, two homes

The simulation is a standalone TypeScript package with no browser or server dependencies. In the editor it runs on the server, which is the authority. In a shipped game there's no editor server, so the same package runs on the player's device.

Writing it once and hosting it twice is why the backend is TypeScript rather than something like Rust: the code that ships to players is the code I test in the editor.

The milestone

Today two fresh browser tabs edited the same scene on the server at once. One tab was refreshed mid-edit and lost nothing, and undo worked across both tabs. Then I pressed Play in one tab and watched the simulation from the other, through a full stop and restart of the backend.

It doesn't look like much in a screenshot, but everything else stands on it: the editor is a window onto a world the server owns, and that world survives the window closing.

A scene for every feature

Every feature also goes into one scene, Re-Forged, so new work can be seen rather than read about. This is how it looked in its first week: a handful of lights, shiny materials, particle fire and smoke, and a camera rail for fly-throughs. It will grow with everything that lands.

State streaming keeps the renderer in the browser. The server runs the authoritative simulation (physics, behaviour, game rules) and sends compact updates about what changed; the browser draws them locally and sends edits back. The research I did put that at a few hundred times less bandwidth than video, with no server GPU per viewer and a UI that responds at local speed.

Prometheus streams state.

One simulation, two homes

The simulation is a standalone TypeScript package with no browser or server dependencies. In the editor it runs on the server, which is the authority. In a shipped game there's no editor server, so the same package runs on the player's device.

Writing it once and hosting it twice is why the backend is TypeScript rather than something like Rust: the code that ships to players is the code I test in the editor.

The milestone

Today two fresh browser tabs edited the same scene on the server at once. One tab was refreshed mid-edit and lost nothing, and undo worked across both tabs. Then I pressed Play in one tab and watched the simulation from the other, through a full stop and restart of the backend.

It doesn't look like much in a screenshot, but everything else stands on it: the editor is a window onto a world the server owns, and that world survives the window closing.

A scene for every feature

Every feature also goes into one scene, Re-Forged, so new work can be seen rather than read about. This is how it looked in its first week: a handful of lights, shiny materials, particle fire and smoke, and a camera rail for fly-throughs. It will grow with everything that lands.

item.title: The game behind the engine
item.description:
Before the engine posts start, here's what all of it is for.

Forgotten Memories, Endless Abyss is an online MMO built around one shared goal: dive as deep and as far as possible. Humanity has found a dungeon that seems to have no bottom. It's so vast that towns have sprung up just to keep adventurers supplied, and everyone is chasing the same questions. Does it end? Why does it exist? Is there a story beneath it all?

A dungeon that reads its players

The dungeon isn't just procedurally generated; it's behaviourally generated. It watches what its players do, in aggregate, and reshapes its landscapes, difficulty and monsters to match. Every layer sits somewhere between order and anarchy.

  • Order comes from cooperation, guild work and players policing each other. Monster pressure eases, towns grow, and blighted ground heals into livable land.
  • Anarchy comes from player-killing and hostility. Spawns get nastier, the terrain degrades toward a hellscape, and town defences can be overrun.

Anarchy spreads like a sickness: one pocket, then many, then faster and faster. A layer that flips blocks fast travel through it and creeps back up toward the shallower layers, so griefing on a deep floor becomes everyone's emergency. Nothing is permanently solved. A paradise left alone can fall again.

You can't die, but you can forget

There's no permadeath. Every revival costs you something instead: fragments of memory. Abilities you've earned can weaken with each revival until they're gone, becoming Forgotten Memories. You feel yourself slipping before anything is lost outright.

The way to get them back is to go deeper. Clearing the dungeon and discovering new layers recovers what death took, so loss pushes you forward rather than back toward safety. That's the title: the endless abyss is the dungeon, and Forgotten Memories are what it costs you, and what it repays.

Holding the line

Roughly every ten layers a raid boss blocks the way. Beat it and travel to that depth unlocks for everyone. But bosses come back. As one nears its return, monsters surge until the layer breaks out in a stampede, and an ignored break loses that layer, then the ones above it, one by one. The frontier and the homeland are the same responsibility.

Towns need supplying too. Players haul materials to keep them running, and an under-supplied town dries up and loses its services. Guilds form around defence, expansion, exploration or policing, and a big enough guild can hold a layer, for a while.

There's more under the surface than this, and some of it is meant to be discovered by players rather than read in a devlog, so I'll leave it there.

Why build an engine for it

A world like this needs things an off-the-shelf engine doesn't hand you: a server that owns the simulation for everyone, the same simulation running on the player's device in a shipped game, and a pipeline that turns 3D models into the pixel-art sprites that live in its 3D dungeon. It also has to run well on phones.

So I'm building Prometheus, a custom 2.5D engine and editor on an all-open-source stack with no vendor royalties. The next posts are about that.
